questions.q: Per this lesson, what three conditions make a re-run 'worth doing'?
options: It's targeted at a specific identified confound, fits the remaining time budget, and would meaningfully change the honest conclusion
It is requested by the hardware provider
It produces a result closer to the original hypothesis, regardless of cause
It uses a completely different qubit count than any prior run
questions.explain: The lesson lists these three conditions explicitly: targeted at a specific fixable confound, fits inside the remaining time budget, and would meaningfully change what can honestly be concluded.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a 'targeted re-run' and an 'open-ended re-run,' per this lesson?
options: A targeted re-run changes exactly one identified confound with everything else fixed; an open-ended re-run has no specific hypothesis about what changed
A targeted re-run always uses more qubits than an open-ended one
An open-ended re-run is always faster to execute
There is no real difference between the two
questions.explain: The lesson defines a targeted re-run as fixing one specific, diagnosed confound while holding everything else constant, versus an open-ended re-run that risks burning time without resolving the actual ambiguity.

questions.q: What does the lesson say you should do with the original run's data and log entry when you decide to iterate?
options: Keep it and add the new run as a new, clearly labeled entry -- don't overwrite or delete the earlier attempt
Delete it immediately to avoid confusion
Merge it silently into the new run's data with no distinction
Report only the new run's result and never mention the earlier one
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly recommends preserving the original data and logging the new run as a distinct, labeled entry, since the report may end up citing both to show the confound's effect and the corrected comparison.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say citing BOTH the original and the corrected result in the final report can be more informative than citing only the corrected one?
options: It demonstrates the confound was actually diagnosed and controlled for, rather than just getting a different number with no explanation
Because reporting two numbers is always required by journals
Because the original result is always more accurate than the corrected one
Because citing both numbers avoids having to compute a significance check
questions.explain: The lesson states that showing both results demonstrates real diagnostic work (identifying and controlling for a confound) rather than simply reporting a different number with no explanation of why it changed.

questions.q: In the check-yourself scenario (one remaining round of hardware runs, choice between a targeted same-window retry and adding an unplanned third qubit count), which choice does this lesson's reasoning support?
options: The targeted same-window retry, since it directly addresses a diagnosed confound rather than introducing new, unplanned scope
Adding a third qubit count, since more data is always better regardless of planning
Neither option, since no further runs should ever be attempted
Both options simultaneously, regardless of the stated time budget
questions.explain: Adding an unplanned third qubit count is exactly the kind of scope creep Lesson 13 warned against, while the targeted retry is a deliberate, diagnosed fix that fits the remaining budget -- the lesson's reasoning favors the targeted option.
